title: Part 1, Chapter 16
paragraphs: Of what happened to the ingenious gentleman in the inn that he took to be a castle

The innkeeper, seeing Don Quixote slung across the ass, asked Sancho what was the matter with him. Sancho answered that it was nothing, only that he had fallen down from a rock and bruised his ribs a little. The innkeeper had a wife whose disposition was not the kind usually found in women of her profession, for she was kind-hearted by nature and felt for the sufferings of her neighbours, so she at once set about tending to Don Quixote, and made her young daughter — a very pretty girl — help her care for their guest. There was besides in the inn, as a servant, an Asturian lass with a broad face, flat back of the head, and snub nose, blind in one eye and not very sound in the other. The elegance of her shape, to be sure, made up for all her defects: she was not seven palms from head to foot, and her shoulders, which weighed down on her somewhat, made her look at the ground more than she liked. This graceful lass, then, helped the young girl, and the two of them made up a very bad bed for Don Quixote in a garret that showed every sign of having served for many years as a hayloft. In it there was also lodged a carrier whose bed was placed a little beyond our Don Quixote's, and which — though made up only of the pack-saddles and cloths of his mules — was much better than Don Quixote's. His consisted simply of four rough boards on two unsteady trestles; a mattress so thin it might have passed for a quilt, full of lumps which, if the rents had not shown them to be wool, would have felt like pebbles in hardness; two sheets of stiff buckler leather; and a coverlet whose threads anyone who chose could have counted without missing one.

On this miserable bed Don Quixote stretched himself out, and the hostess and her daughter soon covered him with plasters from head to foot, while Maritornes — for that was the Asturian's name — held the light for them. While plastering him, the hostess, noticing how full of wheals Don Quixote was in some places, remarked that they looked more like blows than the result of a fall.

It was not blows, Sancho said, but the rock had many points and projections, each of which had left its mark. "Please, señora," he added, "see if you can save some tow, since there's no shortage of someone to use it: my own loins are rather sore too."
"Then you must have fallen as well," said the hostess.
"I did not fall," said Sancho Panza, "but from the shock I got at seeing my master fall, my body aches so much that I feel as if I'd had a thousand thwacks."
"That may well be," said the young girl, "for I've often dreamed I was falling down from a tower and never coming to the ground, and when I woke I felt as weak and shaken as if I had really fallen."
"There is the point, señora," replied Sancho Panza, "that I, without dreaming at all, but being more awake than I am now, find myself with scarcely fewer wheals than my master Don Quixote."
"What is the gentleman called?" asked Maritornes the Asturian.
"Don Quixote of La Mancha," answered Sancho Panza, "and he is a knight-adventurer, and one of the best and stoutest that have been seen in the world this long while past."
"What is a knight-adventurer?" said the lass.

"Are you so new in the world as not to know?" answered Sancho Panza. "Well then, sister, you must know that a knight-adventurer is something that in two words is seen drubbed and emperor — today the most miserable and needy creature in the world, and tomorrow will have two or three crowns of kingdoms to give to his squire."
"Then how is it," said the hostess, "that belonging to so good a master as this, you don't, judging by appearances, even have so much as a county?"

"It's too soon yet," answered Sancho, "for we have only been a month on the road in quest of adventures, and so far we haven't met with anything that can be called one. But it happens that when one thing is looked for, another thing is found; and if my master Don Quixote gets well of this wound, or fall, and I am left no worse off for it, I wouldn't trade my hopes for the best title in Spain."

Don Quixote was listening very attentively to all this conversation, and sitting up in bed as best he could, he took the hostess by the hand and said to her, "Believe me, fair lady, you may count yourself fortunate in having sheltered my person in this castle of yours — a person so distinguished that, if I do not praise myself, it is only because self-praise debases, as the saying goes; but my squire will tell you who I am. I only say that I shall keep forever inscribed in my memory the service you have rendered me, so I may give you my thanks for as long as life shall last me; and would to Heaven that Love did not hold me so enthralled and subject to its laws, and to the eyes of that beautiful ingrate whose name I murmur between my teeth, so that the eyes of this lovely damsel might be the masters of my freedom."

The hostess, her daughter, and the worthy Maritornes listened in bewilderment to the words of the knight-errant, for they understood about as much as if he had been speaking Greek, though they could see that they were all meant for expressions of goodwill and courtesy. Not being used to this kind of language, they stared at him and marvelled to themselves, for he seemed to them a man of a quite different sort from those they were used to; and thanking him in tavern phrases for his civility, they left him, while the Asturian gave her attention to Sancho, who needed it no less than his master.

The carrier had made an arrangement with her for a little recreation that night, and she had given him her word that when the guests were quiet and the family asleep she would come to find him and meet his wishes with no reserve. It is said of this good lass that she never made promises of this kind without keeping them, even when made in a forest and with no witness present, for she prided herself greatly on being a lady, and held it no disgrace to be employed as servant in an inn, since she said that misfortunes and bad luck had brought her to that position. The hard, narrow, miserable, rickety bed of Don Quixote stood first in the middle of this star-lit stable, and close beside it Sancho made his — merely a rush mat and a blanket that looked more like threadbare canvas than wool. Next to these two beds was that of the carrier, made up, as has been said, of the pack-saddles and all the trappings of the two best of his mules, though he had twelve of them — sleek, plump, and in prime condition, for he was one of the rich carriers of Arévalo, according to the author of this history, who particularly mentions this carrier because he knew him very well, and is even said to have been in some degree a relation of his. Besides, Cid Hamete Benengeli was a historian of great research and accuracy in everything, as is very evident, since he would not pass over in silence the trifles already mentioned, however small and insignificant — an example which might well be followed by those grave historians who relate things so curtly and briefly that we hardly get a taste of them, all the substance of the work being left in the inkstand from carelessness, perverseness, or ignorance. A thousand blessings on the author of "Tablante de Ricamonte" and the one who wrote that other book recounting the deeds of Conde Tomillas — with what minuteness they describe everything!

To proceed: after paying a visit to his team and giving them their second feed, the carrier stretched himself on his pack-saddles and lay waiting for his conscientious Maritornes. Sancho by now was plastered up and had lain down, and though he tried to sleep, the pain in his ribs would not let him; while Don Quixote, with the pain in his, had his eyes as wide open as a hare's.

The inn was all silent, and in the whole of it there was no light except that of a lantern that hung burning in the middle of the gateway. This strange stillness, together with the thoughts always present in our knight's mind — of the incidents described at every turn in the books that were the cause of his misfortune — conjured up in his imagination as extraordinary a delusion as can well be conceived: he fancied that he had reached a famous castle (for, as has been said, every inn he lodged in was a castle to his eyes), and that the innkeeper's daughter was the daughter of the lord of the castle, who, won by his courtly bearing, had fallen in love with him and promised to come to his bed for a while that night without her parents' knowledge. Holding all this fantasy he had constructed as solid fact, he began to feel uneasy and to consider the perilous risk his virtue was about to face, and he resolved in his heart to commit no treason against his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, even if Queen Guinevere herself and the dame Quintañona should present themselves before him.

While he was taken up with these fancies, the time and the hour — an unlucky one for him — arrived for the Asturian to come. In her smock, barefoot, with her hair gathered into a fustian coif, with noiseless and cautious steps she entered the room where the three were quartered, in search of the carrier. But she had scarcely reached the door when Don Quixote noticed her, and sitting up in his bed in spite of his plasters and the pain in his ribs, he stretched out his arms to receive his beautiful damsel. The Asturian, doubled up and silent, was groping with her hands before her in search of her lover when she ran into Don Quixote's arms; he grasped her tightly by the wrist, and drawing her towards him while she dared not utter a word, made her sit down on the bed. He felt her smock, and although it was sackcloth, it seemed to him the finest, softest silk; on her wrists she wore some glass beads, but to him they had the sheen of precious Oriental pearls; her hair, somewhat resembling a horse's mane, he rated as threads of the brightest gold of Araby, whose radiance dimmed the sun himself; her breath, which no doubt smelt of yesterday's stale salad, seemed to him to diffuse a sweet aromatic fragrance from her mouth. In short, he drew her portrait in his imagination in the same features and the same style as he had read of other princesses in his books, who, smitten by love, came with all the adornments here described to see a sorely wounded knight. So great was the poor gentleman's blindness that neither touch, nor smell, nor anything else about the good lass — which would have made anyone but a carrier vomit — was enough to undeceive him. On the contrary, he was convinced he had the goddess of beauty in his arms, and holding her firmly in his grip, he went on in a low, tender voice:

"Would that I were, lovely and exalted lady, in a position to repay so great a favour as that which you, by the sight of your great beauty, have granted me. But fortune, never tired of persecuting the good, has chosen to lay me on this bed, where I lie so bruised and broken that, although my inclination would gladly comply with yours, it is impossible. Besides, to this impossibility is added another still greater: the faith I have pledged to the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, sole lady of my most secret thoughts; and were it not for that, I should not be so insensible a knight as to miss the happy opportunity which your great goodness has offered me."

Maritornes was fretting and sweating to find herself held so fast by Don Quixote, and neither understanding nor caring about the words he addressed to her, she struggled without speaking to free herself. The worthy carrier, whose unholy thoughts kept him awake, had been aware of his doxy the moment she came in the door, and was listening attentively to all that Don Quixote said. Jealous that the Asturian should have broken her word with him for another, he drew closer to Don Quixote's bed and stood still to see what would come of this talk he could not understand; but when he saw the wench struggling to get free and Don Quixote striving to hold her, not relishing the joke, he raised his arm and delivered such a terrible cuff on the lank jaws of the amorous knight that he bathed his whole mouth in blood. Not content with that, he climbed on top of his ribs and trampled all over them at a pace rather smarter than a trot. The bed, which was somewhat crazy and not very firm on its legs, unable to support the additional weight of the carrier, came crashing to the ground. At this great noise the innkeeper woke up and at once concluded that it must be some brawl of Maritornes', because after calling loudly to her he got no answer. With that suspicion he got up, lit a lamp, and hurried to the quarter where he had heard the disturbance. The wench, seeing her master coming and knowing how terrible his temper was, frightened and panic-stricken, made for the bed of Sancho Panza, who was still asleep, and crouched on it making a ball of herself.

The innkeeper came in shouting, "Where are you, strumpet? Of course this is some of your doing." At this Sancho woke up, and feeling this mass almost on top of him, fancied he had the nightmare and began throwing fisticuffs all round, a certain share of which fell on Maritornes; who, irritated by the pain and flinging modesty aside, paid back so many in return to Sancho that she woke him fully in spite of himself. He, finding himself so handled by he knew not whom, raised himself up as well as he could, grappled with Maritornes, and between the two of them began the bitterest and funniest scrimmage in the world. The carrier, however, seeing by the light of the innkeeper's candle how it was going with his ladylove, abandoned Don Quixote and ran to bring her the help she needed; and the innkeeper did the same, but with a different intention — for his was to chastise the lass, since he believed beyond doubt that she alone was the cause of all this concert. And so, as the saying is, cat to rat, rat to rope, rope to stick: the carrier pounded Sancho, Sancho the lass, she him, and the innkeeper her, and they all worked away so briskly that they didn't give themselves a moment's rest. The best of it was that the innkeeper's lamp went out, and being left in the dark, they all laid on one another in a mass so unmercifully that there was not a sound spot left where a hand might land.

It so happened that lodging in the inn that night was an officer of what they call the Old Holy Brotherhood of Toledo, who, also hearing the extraordinary noise of the conflict, seized his staff and the tin case with his warrants and made his way in the dark into the room, crying, "Hold! In the name of the Jurisdiction! Hold! In the name of the Holy Brotherhood!"

The first man he came upon was the battered Don Quixote, stretched senseless on his back upon his broken-down bed; and his hand, falling on the beard as he felt about, he continued to cry, "Help for the Jurisdiction!" But noticing that the man he had laid hold of did not move or stir, he concluded that he was dead and that those in the room were his murderers. With this suspicion he raised his voice still louder, calling out, "Shut the inn gate; see that no one goes out; they have killed a man here!" This cry startled them all, and each dropped the fight at the point at which the voice reached him. The innkeeper retreated to his room, the carrier to his pack-saddles, the lass to her crib; the unlucky Don Quixote and Sancho alone were unable to move from where they were. The officer let go Don Quixote's beard and went out to look for a light to search for and apprehend the culprits; but not finding one — for the innkeeper had purposely put out the lantern when he retreated to his room — he was forced to fall back on the hearth, where after much time and trouble he lit another lamp.
